You generally shouldn’t refuse to move out as leverage—even if you believe your landlord owes you back—because holding over usually creates new legal problems rather than solving this one. The retrieved passage notes security deposits are typically held “as an escrow deposit” until premises are surrendered in good condition [Source: Lease], but it doesn’t say tenants can withhold possession themselves when disputes arise. In almost every jurisdiction, refusing to vacate after the lease ends is treated differently from a dispute about how much should be returned; landlords often have broad rights to repossess property once tenancy terminates, and they may charge additional fees or pursue eviction for what’s called “holding over.”

That said, being owed money isn’t your fault—you’re right that you shouldn’t just accept losing your deposit if there was no damage beyond ordinary wear and tear. But withholding physical access usually backfires because it gives them grounds to claim breach of contract on top of any other issues. If you’ve already moved out but they haven’t processed the return within their legal timeframe (often 14–30 days depending on location), small claims court is typically faster than trying to force entry yourself.

Practical steps:
- Document everything: move-out inspection photos/videos from when you left, dated messages where you requested the refund with specific dates referenced in local law, copies of receipts for repairs you made or paid for that relate to damages.
- Send a final written demand citing your state/country’s statutory timeline and attaching evidence—this often prompts payment without further conflict.
- If they refuse after this, file in small claims; courts usually side with tenants who followed proper procedures over those who tried self-help remedies like refusing to leave.
